MR. COLD WELL-PRESS REPORT AS TO MEMBERS' ACCOUNTS WITH KING'S PRINTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the business of the house proceeds I wish to raise a question which affects not only my own privileges but the privileges of the members of this house. Appearing in the Ottawa Journal of last evening was a statement of alleged non-payment of account by me to the king's printer. It was not only published in the local press but went all across the country over the C.B.C. last night. I think other members are in the same position as myself. I was alleged to be in arrears to the amount of $6.25 as of March 31, 1943. May I say that that account was incurred, $3.25 on March 6, 1943 and $3 on March 19, 1943; therefore I was in arrears to the amount of $6.25 as of March 31, 1943. That was unpaid on May 15, but, together with some other small accounts, was paid by cheque in full on July 12, during the session of last year. The impression that has been given to the country is that a large number of members of this house are in debt to the king's printer. I know that some others are in the same position as myself. We owe nothing to the king's printer. We keep our accounts paid regularly as the bills are rendered, and I think, Mr. Speaker, in fairness to the members of the house, the Ottawa Journal, which published the story, and the broadcasting corporation, should make a correction of the wrong impression which was left on the public mind.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to be permitted to clear before the house and the country the name of a very prominent Canadian, who is not in the house at the moment, from any unjustifiable impression that may have been created in the public mind as a result of the reports to which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has referred. I have this telegram from the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, former Prime Minister of Canada:
Am informed government officials have published statement representing me as owing printing bureau some $171 since 1925. Have never known or heard of this alleged debt until to-day. My secretaries then and since say they similarly had no knowledge of any such claim. All printing ordered by me or on my authority or with my knowledge was paid for. Numerous accounts have been rendered me since by bureau and paid with no claim made for past balance. Under these circumstances consider it an outrage that my name should be blazoned through Canada as a defaulting debtor. Please read this telegram to the House of Commons.
Arthur Meighen
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, politics makes strange bedfellows. I have not read the Journal of last night; I very seldom read the papers, but when I came up to the house I met charitable friends who were ready to organize a subscription for an amount of $85 that I have allegedly owed to the king's printer since 1925, 1926 or 1927- a long time ago. Well, I am ready to pay all the debts that I owe, but the taxes are so high that we must proceed gradually. Besides that, Mr. Speaker, it takes a \ irgin soul to be scandalized at such trifling matters. Of course when a man owes some money he has to pay it, as much as he can, but when there is nothing, the king loses all rights. I will tell you one thing, sir, so long as speeches made in the house are broadcast throughout the country through the printing bureau, what is the harm in that?-because the press does not mention them. If the press fulfilled its duty of report* ing speeches of members of parliament there would be no accounts standing at the king's printing bureau. It scandalizes me the more because speeches made by cabinet ministers, even by the former leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), and, I think, by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) especially those made on the plebiscite, have been published at the country's expense. I do not see why speeches made by cabinet ministers should be paid for by the country while hon. members are bled white to pay for a small number of copies of their speeches to inform their constituents of the work they have been doing here.

Mr. Speaker, I now have the full text of Lord Beaverbrook's statement in the House of Lords, made on Wednesday, and as it differs slightly from the agreed statement which I read to the house yesterday, perhaps I should place this version on Hansard. It is sent from the High Commissioner for Canada in London to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and is as follows:
The United States proposed that we should go forward to an international conference on certain lines and I will quote those lines. They were that there should be an international authority to lay down standards for technical requirements and for rates of air carriage and to interchange information. According to the American plan the proposed authority would start on a non-executive basis with no power or means of enforcing its regulations, at least during an interim period. I hope I have made quite clear the position taken up by the United States of America. It proposed an international authority on a non-executive basis with no

power or means of enforcing its regulations at least during the interim period. The United Kingdom delegation presented for consideration what is known as the Canadian draft convention, which has been laid on the table of the Canadian parliament. This draft convention lays down a detailed plan for international regulatory authority with powers of enforcement. Its provisions include the allocation of frequencies of air service and national quotas for international air traffic. I hope I have made clear the distinction between the two proposals. The Canadian proposal was considered by the Americans to be too rigid as a basis for talks at the proposed international conference. After discussion it was agreed, therefore, that we should go forward to the conference on the basis of proposals for international handling of civil aviation agreed at the commonwealth conversations some six months ago. These proposals are in some respects open to varying interpretations and were considered by the Americans to be flexible enough to provide a more satisfactory basis for an international conference. The broad purpose would be to draw' up an international convention on air navigation to be implemented by an international transport organization which would evolve standards, seek to eliminate uneconomic competition, work out for each nation an equitable participation in world air transport and maintain broad equilibrium between air transport capacity and traffic on offer. On these general principles the United States and Great Britain are in agreement. The powers of enforcement of the provisions will be open to further discussion. There you have the progress towards international "cooperation in civil aviation. I repeat the principles, the elimination of uneconomic competition, the setting up of national quotas in international air transport, equilibrium between the transport capacity and the traffic offering on any international air route. These must be the foundations of an enlightened approach to this subject in the future. But make no mistake; we did not give up the Canadian draft convention without reluctance. We would have preferred it. Mr. Howe, the Canadian minister, has produced an admirable document building up his structure for the regulating authority on the principles agreed at the commonwealth conversations.

I have just a few words to say about censorship. In the first place, we asked for a copy of the censorship regulations but it was never tabled. There are, of course, the defence regulations that must be

War Appropriation-War Services
observed by the press, as by any individual; they are for the protection of the country in time of war, as is censorship itself. Lord Macmillan, who was the first British censor, held the view that the news which should be withheld from the public was that which would be detrimental to the war effort, not at all that which w'as in criticism of the government. It is a great mistake for legitimate criticism to be considered a personal insult by any minister; it shows how far away we are from true democratic principles. The idea of having all heads shaped in the same mould is absolutely totalitarian; for only by constructive criticism can we improve the standard, quality and efficiency of the war effort.
Having said that much, I protest most strongly against the actions of the so-called liaison officers of all departments who prevent the press from publishing news which is of value as well as interest to the Canadian people. I remember that at the beginning of the war the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was crazy enough to carry an address which was delivered by Adolf Hitler in Germany. That was most stupid; it was German propaganda carried by the C.B.C., one agency of government, and passed by the board of censors, another agency of government. Against that sort of propaganda I protest most strongly. There is an old Latin axiom which is well known; it is "errare humanum est"-to err is human. We have before us, if we will raise our heads and look before us, the one great cause which justifies and ennobles everything we have ever said and thought. We have greater right to believe in ourselves and in the victory of the things we fight for now than we have ever had before in our lifetime. If we will believe, if we will act on our belief, nothing, no organization of reaction and ignorance, no political stultification, no power whatever of selfishness and cowardice and doubt, can stand against us.
To accept the inevitability of reaction at this point in the history of our world and of our cause-to accept and to submit to the swing_ of the pendulum-to bow our heads to the wind that blows the candles out-to surrender in advance of the attack-is not faint-heartedness alone, but folly.

I have heard a lot of discussion under the minister's estimates as to the maintenance and promotion of national unity, but this type of advertising which I am going to read for the minister's benefit is a type of advertising from which the province of Nova Scotia, and particularly the mining sections, have suffered for the past fifty years. It

certainly does nothing to promote national unity. This Canadian Press dispatch reads as follows:
Their pockets bulging with lump-sum wage increases, coal miners of Sydney Mines and nearby Florence have been on a $160,000 buying spree since the weekend, and neither of the two collieries in the towns has worked since Friday.
Christmas business paled beside this rush to the store counters, merchants reported, as their cash registers tinkled merrily. Saturday night's volume of business was the biggest in years.
Liquor stores did a brisk business Monday, and there were reports that as high as thirty-six dollars was paid bootleggers for a dozen quarts of beer.
The celebration was expected to end to-night, with the miners resuming regular operations to-morrow.
About fifteen hundred miners shared in the windfall, which came through retroactive pay increases going back to November 1, 1943, under an order of the national ivar labour board.
Knowing the situation as it exists, I think the Canadian Press dispatch should have been thrown into the wastebasket somewhere in central Canada., because it does not tell the true story. It is distorted, misleading, and deliberate propaganda to prejudice the rest of Canada against the coal miners in that end of the country, and miners generally. The Canadian Press representative who wrote that dispatch has done a disservice to that part of the country and has thrown mud in the eyes of the Canadian people. The statement, made in glaring headlines, that the miners' pockets are bulging with money is deliberate propaganda. If anyone stopped to think about the matter he would realize that. Fifteen hundred miners participated in that retroactive payment of $160,000. That works out at exactly $107 per man. The majority of these men are married. For two years the Nova Scotia miners of this particular group carried on negotiations through their executive board with the war labour board, while their lontract was in abeyance; for two years they negotiated for that increase of wages, which was granted in December, 1943, and from then to date they have waited for payment; and I am safe in saying that ninety-five per cent of the money which was received on this account was owed by the miners and earmarked for payment of their debts before they received it.
A little further in the story the writer says that the mines were idle. Reading that statement, the reader who does not know the situation is led to believe that from Friday until Monday every one of those fifteen hundred miners, their families and friends, were around making whoopee and there was no coal being produced. That is not the situation at all. For many years the coal mines of Nova

Scotia have not been worked on Saturday. The five-day week was in operation. Not very much coal has been produced on Saturdays since the outbreak of the war, as the end of the week is generally a clean-up time. Friday night is practically the end of the coal-producing week. Saturday is the only day when the miners have a chance to clean up properly and enjoy perhaps a few hours' sunshine. We must remember that these people live half of their lives underground. And Saturday is not the same as it is in this province. There are no beer parlours in Nova Scotia; there is no place in town where one can go and sit down and buy a glass of beer. Intoxicants are sold only by the government liquor store, and on Saturday, the only day when the miner has a chance to get a bottle of beer, the liquor stores are not open. One can get a fairly good idea of how much of this money went into liquor when it is realized that there is nowhere to purchase it. The stores are closed when the men get home in the evenings, and-
Are there no bootleggers there?

That is the point I am coming to. On Saturday, the day they are home, the store is closed. I am not as bad-minded as the ex-leader of the opposition. Whether the government of the province enacted their liquor laws in the interests of the bootlegger is something I am not prepared to say.
I want to make this matter clear to hon. members, because there is too much of this kind of propaganda. Inquire of the Department of National War Services, and you will find that in the matter of voluntary enlistments no section of Canada surpasses the coal mining districts of Nova Scotia. At the present time these men are frozen to their jobs. If you were looking for voluntary enlistments in that end of the country you could fill your quota in twenty-four hours and close your offices the next day. As regards victory loans, within two or three days the quota for the coal mining districts of Nova Scotia is subscribed one hundred per cent. Never up to date have they gone under; they have always gone over their quota, and they have got it quickly. They have a systematic organization; they know the job has to be done, and the job is done. As I have said, their war record is not surpassed in any other part of this country.
If the man who wrote that Canadian Press dispatch is in Sydney, he knows the facts as well as I do. That is why I am objecting so strongly to this story emanating from that section of the country. You may have ninety-eight per cent of your working force in a

coal mine report for duty in the morning, ready to mine coal, but there is a classification of boys who work on the haulages, who grab that coal to the rope, and who represent perhaps less than one-half of one per cent of the employees; but if half a dozen of them are off they cannot be replaced, and the result is that the mine is tied up. If a very few drivers who handle the coal by horses underground are absent from work, the mine cannot operate. The writer of the dispatch would lead one to believe that all the men in the colliery during the one day it was idle were on a drunken spree, forgetting their obligations to the country. The fact is that half a dozen boys who are in good positions, who have special training for a dangerous type of work, and who are the only ones permitted to handle it, can tie up the mine if they are off work. The writer of that press dispatch deliberately designed it, in my opinion, to create a wrong impression of the miners to the general public with respect to that particular class of people. If anything can cause dissatisfaction or indifference to the war effort in that particular section of the country, it is this kind of advertising, which is designed for the wrong purposes and certainly does not promote national unity. I bring it to the attention of the Minister of National War Services because I think he should check with the Canadian Press, and if there is any necessity for censorship I think it is indicated in the item I have read. Some of our papers
operate as a free press; there is no question that most of them do. But I could name papers that do not. Another paper in the province of Quebec that I could mention, L'Action Catholique, does exactly the same. That is not a free press. I can understand a party press confining its columns to its party. In Saskatchewan there

is the Saskatchewan Liberal. I do not know where they get the paper to publish this little sheet, which circulates in the thousands. I would not expect to see in the Saskatchewan Liberal a speech of mine published correctly, but that is a Liberal party press. My complaint is against some members of the daily press, which is maintained by the public through subscriptions, and by national advertising. Allegedly, we have a free press in this' country, but it is not a free press when we have papers with such a wide circulation as the Montreal Star refusing to publish reports of speeches made by members of one particular party and refusing its advertising. That is the worst kind of financial and economic censorship. So that when we talk of a free press, let us bear in mind that there are exceptions. If hon. members have disposed of the political aspect of this item, I should like to make a few observations concerning censorship. There cannot be two views as to the need of censorship during war time, but there may be differences of opinion as to the type we should have and the degree to which it should be applied. There are two kinds of censorship, the voluntary, and the official type which is governed by regulations. I do not believe that voluntary censorship can work; in my opinion it is no censorship at all. Some people could not keep a secret if they tried. Others have varying opinions as to what is secret and what is not. Then, of course, judgment varies among the various individuals engaged in newspaper work or other types of work in connection with this matter. For instance, a conscientious and cautious editor would leave out a story, whereas an aggressive editor would take chances and dramatize the report to the advantage of his own newspaper. So that there is a definite need of official censorship in time of war, whether it has to do with newspapers, radio, or mail. Official censorship makes for uniformity and consistency.
But, as I said, we should seriously consider how far we should go. My criticism of the government's policy is that there are too many instances of, undignified and at times perhaps abusive censorship. Examples have been related to the committee this afternoon. We all know of instances where the mail of members of parliament was opened. Of course that sort of thing should not be permitted.
My other objection is that certain information is refused to hon. members and is later given to the press. We are somewhat at a loss to know what to tell our constituents; we know so little about the policies or intentions of the government that it is not infrequent that the

Mr. LaFLECHE : If I may be permitted I should like to place on record a statement; it is not lengthy, but I think it will give much of the information required by the hon. member for Camrose, and if necessary I can supplement it.
Experimental broadcasting on a short-wave band began almost simultaneously with experimental broadcasts in Great Britain, the United States and Holland in 1926. The technical development progressed rapidly, and in 1932 the British Broadcasting Corporation inaugurated its empire service with a regularly scheduled service in English. The value of this new instrument of international communication was soon recognized, and the thirties saw a rapid growth of short-wave broadcasting, particularly from Europe. By 1937 fifty-eight countries were broadcasting on a short-wave band, on frequencies registered at Geneva. Certain bands in the spectrum were set aside at Geneva for short-wave broadcasting. The frequencies within these bands were chosen by the different countries on a first come, first served basis. The various countries then registered them at the International Telecommunication Bureau at Geneva.
Nazi Germany and Italy were the first countries to exploit short-wave as a weapon of offensive propaganda. Great Britain which had done a great deal of the pioneering in the short-wave field looked upon short-wave broadcasting primarily as a medium for the promotion of international good will, a philosophy well expressed in the motto of the British Broadcasting Corporation. "Nations shall speak peace unto nations." However, the

tactics of the German propagandists forced Great Britain to take similar action, though it was not until January 3, 1938, that the first foreign language broadcast was carried by British Broadcasting Corporation.
By 1939 Great Britain was broadcasting a regular service in ten foreign languages. With the outbreak of war the British Broadcasting Corporation foreign service was, of course, increased tremendously. Many new high-powered transmitters were put into operation, and by 1941 the British Broadcasting corporation was broadcasting over several stations more than thirty hours a day in some forty-eight languages.
The development of short-wave broadcasting in the United States lagged considerably behind the service inaugurated by the publicly owned systems of Europe. However, when war broke out, the United States began far-reaching plans for the creation of a comprehensive system of high-powered short-wave transmitters. The short wave-transmitters operated by the American networks were taken over by the United States government through the office of war information. New transmitters were constructed as rapidly as possible, and soon the voice of America was heard in many languages on a large network of shortwave transmitters.
In September, 1942, the government of Canada approved the construction of an international short-wave station. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was instructed to proceed with the construction and operation of such a station as soon as possible. The demand for transmitting equipment was so great both in United States and United Kingdom that even with the high priorities granted Canada inevitable delay was encountered in procurement of equipment. However, considerable progress has been made and it is expected that the first beam will be in operation by perhaps September, 1944.
I do not mean by that an international service. The first beam may be in operation by next September. This is questionable, however; it might be a little later in the year.
The first estimates on the cost of the shortwave station submitted by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation quoted a figure of 8800,000 for the purchase and installation of two 50-kilowatt transmitters and the associated antenna system. This expenditure, chargeable to war appropriations, was approved. Owing to changes in design and construction, the result of recent improvements in radio techniques, making for greater efficiency in short-wave transmissions, and owing to the increase in costs of fabrication and construction, it is now estimated that

the required transmitters, antenna, associated equipment and construction will involve an additional capital expenditure of $300,000, making a total estimated cost of $1,100,000.
Most of this increased cost is for a new and more elaborate antenna system which it is expected will have the result of providing a signal equal to that which would have been provided by transmitters four times the power operating on the type of antenna originally considered.
I think the hon. member for Camrose had in mind that in the first year the sum of $10,000 was asked for. Undoubtedly that was for preliminary investigation. Last year the house voted $650,000. It was considered at that time that not more than that amount could be expended in the fiscal year 1943-44. I now ask for $150,000. When the estimates were prepared the officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation thought that amount would be sufficient to cover what they could do. It may be necessary for me to ask the government to bring down a supplementary estimate, if experience proves that the cost will be considerably higher than the original estimate of $800,000. If it is possible to let contracts, arrange construction, obtain equipment, antenna and transmitters we shall have to pay for them.

Mr. LaFLECHE: The amount of $1,100,000 was a revised estimate of the cost. The expenditure is an entirely different matter. The total budget must be in the neighbourhood of $1,100,000.

messages which go over that station will truly reflect to the world at large what sort of a nation we have, and call upon every one of us to do what we can to make this nation worthy of world publicity. The figures with regard to audiences are very interesting. As an example I would point out that about two million persons in Canada see each issue of the series called "World in Action". May I be permitted to place on record a brief yet fairly illustrative statement in regard to the activities of the national film board.
During 1943-44, as in previous years since the outbreak of war, the board has devoted a great part of its energies to the service of war departments of the government, and to a continuation of its own very extensive work in the field of wartime information. On the production side, among the departments which the national film board has served extensively are the three departments of national defence, the Department of Munitions and Supply, the national war finance committee, the wartime prices and trade board, the wartime information board and the Department of Labour. Its own programme of war information in the film field includes a continuation on a regular monthly basis of the two series of twenty-minute films issued under the general titles, "Canada Carries On" and "World in Action." These two series have achieved a remarkably wide theatrical distribution in Canada and abroad, and have earned for the national film board an enviable reputation for excellence in its field. Among the subjects issued1 in the "Canada Carries On" series during the past year have ben such pictures as "Up from the Ranks," "Train Busters," "Target Berlin," "Proudly She Marches," "Coal Face Canada," "Look to the North" and "Thought for Food." The "World in Action" series has included films on "Labour Front," "The War for Men's Minds," "The Fighting Dutch," "The Gates of Italy," "The Battle of Europe" and "Our Northern Neighbour." In additon to the two series I have mentioned, the national film board has continued its extensive service of Canadian pictures to newsreels published throughout the world, and the record in respect of the publication of these stories is a very impressive one. Apart from the French language versions of the "World in Action" and "Canada Carries On" series, a regular service of "Reportages" on matters connected with the war is maintained to French language theatres throughout the province of Quebec.
The distribution systems which have been established for the exhibition of films produced by the national film board and by others among our allies are no less impressive than the production record. The rural circuits, so-called, now serve on a monthly basis some 1,600 communities in the rural areas of Canada with programmes closely related to Canada's war effort, directed particularly, so far as interest is concerned, to agricultural audiences.

War Appropriation-War Services
The industrial circuits reach more than 1,000 factories every month and, in collaboration with the various labour organizations and the workers' educational association, an extensive service to trade unions is maintained. This is in addition to the extensive film library system which is maintained in collaboration with local authorities throughout the country to serve audiences of every sort.
In the foreign field there has also been a gratifying extension of our distribution activity. The "World in Action" series continues to be distributed widely throughout the United States, the United Kingdom, Australasia and many other countries, and certain subjects in the "Canada Carries On" series considered suitable for international distribution have secured wide circulation in the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia and elsewhere. The newsreel stories released by the film board to newsreel editors have been issued throughout the world.
Early in 1943 the national film board assumed certain functions in relation to the production and distribution of still pictures which had formerly been performed by the wartime information board. This service has been continued and extended with highly satisfactory results in respect particularly of the distribution of still pictures in Canada and the United States. The work of the graphics division stills of the national film board has been considerably extended in response to the requirements of the armed services and other war departments. Services in respect of layout of publications, the preparation of photographic exhibits for educational and other purposes and the production of instructional film strips are now available at the national film board to all departments of government requiring these services. They are all being extensively used.
This is a very brief review of the board's activity, but it is enough, I think, to indicate that the work of the board is carried on with imagination and vitality.

The minister mentioned the fact that one of the most successful of the series, known as "The World in Action", had been widely distributed. I do not know what the distribution is in Britain, but in the United States it goes to about five or six thousand theatres every month. So good has this series become that the columnist Dorothy Thompson recently devoted to it a whole section of her column. She said that the film board of Canada had set the world an example in supplying national and international information, something for which the board should receive commendation.
I sincerely hope that it will be part of government policy to continue the work of the film board, which has been done so admirably in war, into the peace period; in other words, to carry on the advertising of Canada. Reference was made once this evening to the advertising which will be done over the air by broadcast, and I think we must not minimize the value of the film in this direction. There is no doubt that by influencing public opinion the film is useful in establishing in the minds of people abroad the fact that Canada is a potential market, and it keeps the channels of public information very well supplied. I

can look back with some amusement at the ideas I had of Canada before I came to this country; they were quite fantastic, although I was probably quite an ordinary product of the British educational system. All over the world people may still have rather strange ideas, if not quite so funny as were my own; but during the war, with our boys going overseas and by other means, people abroad have a better idea of Canada than I had many years ago. Nevertheless to-day, when Canada is the world's third trading nation, we realize that in the future we shall have competition in Europe from both Britain and the United States. Both these countries will use the film as a very popular medium to press their claims for trade and markets, and in this matter Canada must not be left behind. We must do everything in reason to let the people of Europe, Britain and the United States of America know the potentialities of our country, not merely through government departments and bodies of that kind, but through the medium of the film, which gets right to the people.

Films of this kind would link us to the peoples of other countries in very subtle bonds. They would have greater strength, in my opinion, than many material things, and these films also arouse in Canadians a great feeling of pride, to think that they belong to a country which has produced men who loved Canada so intensely and who were capable of reproducing her wild loveliness for the peoples of other nations to see.

In only one area to which I referred, namely, the area on the Hamilton river in Labrador, would there be any troops. All the other places to which I referred are remote areas of northern Ontario and small centres like Chipewyan on lake Athabaska. There would not be over two hundred people there altogether. I have wondered for a long time what means or methods are applied in those remote areas to enable the people to see a picture occasionally.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I take it that the hon. member for Davenport has in mind the civilian population?

Yes.
Mr. LaFLECHE: We have already covered this evening the case of the members of the armed forces. The recreation and amusement of the civilians, of course, is left to private initiative. But the rural film circuits, as I said a moment ago, are being increased in number and extended so as to cover the greater part of Canada, in the hope that before very long the time will come that wherever there is a reasonable number of persons it will be possible to send films to them; but it requires the demand and the cooperation of, say, the two hundred persons in the isolated community mentioned by the hon. member for Davenport. There is a desire on the part of the national film board to do that, but it requires the people concerned in those areas to make known their desires to make it possible to have a showing there.

Would the films be sent free to them?
Mr. LaFLECHE: The films of the rural film circuits are provided without charge, yes.

I am glad that the committee is giving some attention to the rural films. I know that in my part of Canada, Saskatchewan, the work that has been done by the rural film circuits is greatly appreciated by everybody and the films are of a very high order. Unfortunately I was called out of the chamber a few moments ago and was not present at all the discussion. Would the minister give us the number nf projectionists who are undertaking this work in the various rural parts of Canada? While I do not want to ask

War Appropriation-War Services
a number of questions separately because I want to assist in expediting the work of the committee, I should like to ask if the minister could give the committee, if he has not already done so, some outline of the use that is being made of our films in South America, the United States and elsewhere. From time to time in magazines and newspapers, not only those devoted to the film industry but such publications as Time, we have read complimentary references to the documentary and other films that have been put out by the national film board. I was wondering if the minister could give us some idea of the amount of work that has been undertaken, because I believe this service which the film board is rendering, not only to our own rural communities, which is very important, but also to the country at large in making Canada better known in South America, the United States and, of course, Great Britain, is something of which this House of Commons should have greater knowledge and appreciation. After all, the amount of money which is being spent may look very large to some people, but in my opinion the returns the country is getting from this expenditure far exceed the amount of money we are appropriating. I think some of us in this house who appreciate the work that is being done should endeavour to get for ourselves and for the country a clear outline of the valuable work this organization is doing for the dominion as a whole at the present time. To my mind the documentary films that are being made, and the many thousands of feet, I imagine, of film from which these films are being cut, are of great historical value to us.
I have another thought in that connection. Sometimes I wonder as to the wisdom of allowing these valuable documents concerning the war and the war effort to remain in a building which has struck me from time to time as being something of a fire-trap. I think the time has come-perhaps this cannot be done now in the middle of the war, when priorities may be against it-when plans should be laid, with the encouragement of this parliament, for a proper place where these valuable documents may be housed with no danger of being destroyed by fire at some time in the future; and where the facilities for the people who work on the production of these films will reflect some credit upon the country and the orgainzation. Personally, having had some experience in education, I believe that visual education will play a much bigger part in the future than it has done in the past, and that only an organization of the type of which the foundations are now being laid in the national film board can adequately perform the duties

that will be necessary in order to supply our educational institutions with the films that will be required in the future. These very films we are discussing to-night, having to do with the war and Canada's war effort, while they are interesting to our people at the present time will be of much greater interest in the years to come. Twenty, thirty, fifty or one hundred years from now the library of films being built up, and the documents being collected to-day by the national film board, will be of supreme interest; and anything we as a parliament can do to assist in this valuable work should be done.
I asked the minister one or two questions, and I should like to. hear something in reply if the minister is in a position to give it.
Mr. LaFLECHE: The national film board is now operating a total of eighty-two rural film circuits. There is every desire to increase that number as it can be done properly and efficiently; as I said before, it is hoped to be able in due course to cover much more of the rural parts of Canada.
The number of 35 and 16-millimetre films sent out last year from Canada by the national film board to a number of countries, I believe some thirty in all, was 2,503. The list is quite formidable. It may be interesting if I quickly read the list of countries to which the national film board has sent films: the United States, Great Britain, the U.S.S.R., Australia, India, the British West Indies, Newfoundland, New Zealand, South Africa, Egypt, Argentina, Chile, Brazil, Mexico, Cuba, Porto Rico, Greenland, Iceland, Colombia, Panama, Peru, Dominica, Nicaragua, Uruguay, San Salvador, Costa Rica, Venezuela, Ecuador, Honduras and Guatemala.

Any idea how many people see these films or in how many theatres they are shown, both the shorts and the full length films?
Mr. LaFLECHE: We sent these films on request, so that we know they are to meet a demand. We have not a proper report which would enable us to say what have been the audiences to see the different films; I am afraid that would be beyond us.

Could the minister give us an estimate of the number of theatres in which these films are regularly shown?
Mr. LaFLECHE: We know that in the United Kingdom our films are shown in over a thousand theatres and in the United States in over five thousand. We believe that the total of such theatres in all countries would be upwards of eight thousand.

Mr. LaFLECHE: Yes.

How many trained

The hon. member said something about safer quarters. I am very happy to say that as far as possible we have removed all fire hazards from the quarters of the film board on Sussex street in Ottawa. The board hopes that some day it will have a proper building for its head offices, laboratories and factory. Of course there is need for that. Making film is a hazardous occupation, and it is not always agreeable to other business houses to have film made in a neighbouring building; I do not believe the fire underwriters like it very much. Nevertheless it is hoped that some day. not too far distant, there will be safety vaults and good modern buildings to meet the requirements of the national film board.

Are these projectionists on the regular staff of the film board?

Mr. LaFLECHE: I thought it might have been taken for granted that the units were
self-sufficient; otherwise they could not operate. That is made possible by the fact that -some of them generate their own electricity. They have a system to do that, and they are selfsufficient. As a member of the film board, along with my colleague the Minister of National War Services, who is its chairman, I should like very warmly to support the general tenor of the observations made a few moments ago by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar. The Minister of National War Services has given the committee a good deal of detailed information respecting the operations of the board, the countries in which these pictures made in Canada circulate, and approximately the number of people who see them.
Irrespective of our political affiliations I think we can all agree that this is a great service, and that it is well worth while to have Canadian pictures of Canadian scenes, Canadian life and Canadian activities shown regularly in over 5,OQO theatres in the United States and over 1,000 theatres in Great Britain, as well as in theatres in practically every country in the world. I know of nothing which will more effectively broaden in every way the information people desire to have about their neighbours than the agency of films. I think, too, it is an important factor in the promotion of international good will. If we have pictures of Canadian life and Canadian activities shown to the peoples of other countries they come to a clearer understanding and a better knowledge of the kind of country Canada is, and what its people are like.
The more I see of the work done by the film board, the more I am convinced of its great utility to Canada. I wish to pay tribute to those who are actively associated in the work of producing and distributing these pictures. While I do not wish to mention any names, I must say we are very fortunate in

War Appropriation-War Services
having associated with the work of production and distribution people with keen imagination and great energy.
Undoubtedly the film can be made a tremendous agency for sound education. After all, people learn readily through the visual processes, and receive impressions that are probably more lasting and more permanent than might be obtained through reading-or even, Mr. Chairman, than they might learn by listening to speeches in the House of Commons. Therefore the value of this agency is disseminating information can scarcely be measured. I look upon it as an important factor not only in the international sphere, but also as an agency for great good within Canada itself.
In the last forty years I have travelled a good deal over this country. There are not many parts of it which at some time or another I have not visited.
You missed Waterloo.

What has struck me is
this: I may go to the maritime provinces and find that they do not know very much about the problems or the living conditions of people in Alberta. The people of Ontario know comparatively little about -the activity and way of life of, or what the people in British Columbia are thinking about. Newspapers do not circulate much as between these different parts of Canada. I recall being in Vancouver many years ago, and, while there, staying at the Vancouver hotel. I went to the hotel newsstand to buy a Winnipeg paper, but there was not one to be had; nor could I get a Toronto paper.

You went to the wrong
stand.
They may have more since then.
Not much.

But I must say that I
could have bought any one of a dozen United States papers at the same news stand. The thought struck me: How are we to hold this country together? How are we to build up this thing we call national unity-for which I believe there is a definite need, to serve a definite purpose.
Through the agency of films a tremendous amount can be done in that direction. We can have films made showing the activities of the fishermen of Nova Scotia. Those films can be shown on the prairies. We can have films made of the activities of the lumbermen of British Columbia, and they can be shown in Ontario and Quebec. Pictures can be made of rural life in Quebec, and distribution could

be carried out across Canada. We could produce films-we have produced some-showing the potentialities of our great north land, and give our people an understanding of a part of the country concerning which they know very little.
I apologize for taking up this time, because I know the minister is anxious to have his estimates passed, but as a result of my association with the work of the film board in the last few years I am sure there is no vote coming before the committee which I could more willingly support than the one we are now discussing. I doubt if in the long run, particularly in the educational field, there is any vote the expenditure of which is doing more good.

I agree with everything
the minister has said. There is nothing better than a picture to build up in the minds of the people something of the potentialities of Canada. I think the greatest disappointment I ever had in my life was when I first saw a circus. I had seen an elephant in pictures and it was nothing new to me to see one in the circus. I had also seen tigers and lions. While I had never seen monkeys in pictures, I had seen some of them in public life. But the fact of the matter is that the whole thing was spoiled because it was nothing new to me.
I think something such as the minister has suggested is the only thing we can do to teach the people in the different parts of this country to appreciate the other parts. They must be shown films of the different sections of the dominion. People have visualized the Rockies who have never seen the Rockies and never will. People have visualized the valleys and farms and the fisheries and shipping of the maritimes when they will never see them in fact. It is a tremendous job that this film board has to do.
But sometimes I wonder if we are just as honest in connection with these estimates as we ought to be. I think it is nearly time we realized that the people love expenditures, provided that they produce dividends. What do we find in connection with the estimates of the film board? A year or two ago Mr. Grierson, the head of the board, received $6,000. He was then made the head of the wartime information board at an increased salary of $10,000. He was then brought back to the film board, and I understand his salary was the same.
I wonder whether in our desire to try to hide expenditures, in our desire to try to tell the Canadian people what we are doing without letting them know the cost, we are not actually doing more harm than good. There is nothing better than giving the people an

War Appropriation-War Services
honest picture of just what is happening in these matters. I believe that if the government said, ('We are going to find a man who will be able to publicize Canada to Canadians, who can publicize Canada to the world, and we will pay him $15,000 or $20,000, if necessary." I do not think the public generally would criticize such an expenditure which might bring back such large dividends.
This may be done by our ministers in an effort to avoid criticism, but I do not know. The leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation a short time ago questioned whether projectionists were receiving enough money. I question that also. I know something of their activities. I know something of the good that these films have done in our industries and rural schools. None of these men is receiving anything like the wages that are being paid to many workmen in our factories. If there is any authority in this country that ought to set a standard of wages it is the government. The government should pay salaries sufficiently large to bring from private enterprise the best men available.
I do not say this in an attempt to criticize Mr. Grierson. However, I feel that we ought to be truthful with the people and let them know just what the position is. I commend the minister for the work this board is doing, because I think it is a great work and they should expand it. They could go much farther than they have, but I feel we should be frank with the people in so far as the public accounts are concerned.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I hasten to rise to point out to the hon. member for Waterloo South that while it may be innocence on his part, he has done a great wrong to a valued civil servant. In talking about the present film commissioner, Mr. John Grierson, and about hiding of expenditures, I do not think he could have found a more impossible or extravagant illustration. The gentleman he has named was raised to a salary of $10,000 a year in November, 1941. His going to the wartime information board had nothing whatsoever to do with his salary, because he was receiving that salary before he went to that board. He continued to receive the same salary after he finished his term of office with the wartime information board. It must be remembered that Mr. Grierson was not transferred permanently to the wartime information board; he took on that extra work, stating in advance that it would be only for a certain number of months. I am sure the hon. member for Waterloo South will not mind this correction.
In connection with projectionists I stated to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that
they are being paid in accordance with trade union rates or understanding. They receive about S140 a month with cost of living bonus. I agree that this is not a great deal of money, but on the other hand they seem to live well enough. There is no trouble with them and there are many persons who want these positions. It is not a bad life since they move around and see lots of people. I say these things because sometimes a word said in error goes far afield and truth does not catch up to it.

While we cannot compete with so-called enterprise in the payment of salaries, I think if we want to get the best people in the public service we shall have to make conditions more attractive than they are. We cannot continue to employ people in the public service if we underpay them, and that is what we are doing throughout the civil service. When the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture were before us we were discussing veterinary surgeons and we found that the salaries paid were simply scandalous.
I am not so sure that these projectionists are getting trade union rates in terms of a yearly salary. From the few of them I have met, my observation has been that while they receive $140 a month and a certain allowance for their cars, they must provide the cars. If my recollection is correct they are paid about seven cents a mile for gasoline, tires, repairs and so on, but I believe sometimes they use the car engine to generate power and I do not know whether they are paid for that. If they are receiving only $140 a month for doing this kind of work, they are underpaid. In order to have people who can present these films in an acceptable manner you must have persons with some education.
From time to time I have listened to some of these projectionists exhibit films and I have been pleased indeed with the type of men who are doing this work. They were able to present the film in a manner which interested the people who were taking advantage of the particular, rural show. It seems to me that our ideas with regard to educational and cultural activities are all wrong. While we cannot hope to compete with business concerns in the salaries we pay, we should pay sufficient to maintain these people in adequate comfort. When we consider the responsibility entailed in making these films and then compare the remuneration of the chief of the branch or his assistants with the salaries paid by business concerns, we seem to be paying virtually nothing at all. I am not suggesting that we pay fabulous sums, but in all our cultural

War Appropriation-War Services
activities-in films, in broadcasting, and in the realm of education-we ought to give greater encouragement financially and in terms of security than we are giving to-day. I hope that we may be reassessing these cultural activities and that we shall place them on a better footing than they have been. I do not think we are paying anybody connected with the national film board too much; I have no doubt from what I know that we are paying too little, as we are paying too little in so many of our departments. Take our research council; the salaries of our scientists there are something of a public scandal. We have the responsibility of giving greater encouragement to the able and often brilliant young men and women who might be tempted to go into some private industry but who remain in the public service because they wish to develop it as a life work and do something worth while for the country in which they live.

Are rural circuits proportioned to our province according to population? Also, are slides available for educational purposes for the school children? It is difficult to imagine anything more interesting or of more value to school children than each Saturday afternoon to have a showing of the slides of various parts of the provinces and the dominion, in auditoriums and various local schools, and in community halls in rural districts where they never see such a thing as a film and where nevertheless there are good-sized communities, perhaps of two or three hundred people. A private entertainment concern would never go there. This service could be accomplished very readily and at little expense if a certain number of slides were allocated to each community, we will say for Saturday afternoons, upon request of the principal of the high school or of the public school, so that somebody would be responsible. The educational value would be marked.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I am grateful to the hon. member for Kootenay West, and I am sure he will be pleased to know that these rural circuit projectionists do, as a matter of course, give a showing in the afternoon in the local school for the school children when the projectionists go to a given point to provide displays, say in the evening, for She adult population. The point made by my hon. friend is an excellent one. As I said before, the service is being gradually increased as there is demand and, in the case of rural circuits, provincial cooperation.

For instance, if the principal of a high school made a request for a certain number of slides to fill in a programme for Saturday afternoon for educational purposes, 	; - i - j
would the board send those slides? Also, are there any rural circuits in British Columbia? I have never seen one. Nor have I ever seen a display of government films.
Mr. LaFLECHE: There are rural circuits in British Columbia; and as for high school principals or school principals obtaining, I do not say prints, but films, they can be had from what we term the national film board libraries, scattered here and there. If my hon. friend has any particular point in view and would care to write to the film board, his request will receive every possible consideration.

To what extent are
departments of education interested in the kind of thing that the hon. member for Kootenay West has mentioned?
Mr. LaFLECHE:	The provincial departments of education are very much interested in this.

Are plans being worked out? I think every school nowadays should have a machine. Many schools, of course, with which I am acquainted have them.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I could hardly undertake that the national film board would provide them.

Oh, I do not mean that. I do not want to be misunderstood. I mean that every school district should provide itself with a machine.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I agree.

Then, perhaps, through the national film board, a series of still pictures, slides, and films could be provided and could circulate like a library from school to school.
Mr. LaFLECHE: Right now the film board is working along those lines. We have already established film libraries; and, to make it practical, if anyone interested would care to write, every assistance would be afforded.

I heartily concur in all the remarks which have been made with respect to the educational work of the film board. I believe the time is not far distant when a great deal of our education will be imparted through the medium of the film. I have two small questions to ask the minister. The first is, could he give me the number of schools in each province? The second is, what constitutes a circuit?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I am sorry that I have not the eighty-two circuits broken down by provinces. This may be interesting: The cost

War Appropriation-War Services
of operating the circuits wholly financed by the board is approximately $375 per circuit per month. This sum provides the salary and expenses of the projectionist, shipping charges, print costs, maintenance of equipment, and publicity. If my hon. friend wants to know how many circuits there are in Saskatchewan I shall get the details and send them to him.

I am more interested in Alberta than in Saskatchewan. But if the minister would bring down figures for all the provinces, not this evening but at some other time, they might be put on Hansard.
Mr. LaFLECHE: With pleasure.

I should like to know the number of circuits in each province, and also the average number of points that axe covered in a circuit.
Mr. LaFLECHE: Each circuit comprises at least twenty different points a month. But I shall bring down this information.

I do not like to delay the committee, but a statement was made by the Minister of Mines and Resources which I do not feel like allowing to pass without contradiction. Speaking of my own province, he stated that he could not find on the news stands any newspapers from Winnipeg or Toronto. As for the minister not being able to get a newspaper from Winnipeg or Toronto, I guarantee that I could take him to fifty news stands which would give him any paper he wants from any province.

I can assure the hon. member for New Westminster that the statement I made was a correct one. My visit on that occasion was a good many years ago. I am delighted to know that the west coast has made such substantial progress since that time.
In forty-five years?
Shall the item carry? Carried.
Are we under sundries?

I did not quite catch the carrying of that item. I was going to ask about trade union films, because I think we should have some knowledge of what is being done in that regard. I believe a great
deal has been done in the past by the showing of films and so on, and I think we should try to get a picture of this both for ourselves and for the country through the record. There have, I believe, been industrial and trade union circuits. What are they, And what do they do?

Is there any guarantee-
Mr. LaFLECHE: There should be a correct description and all the necessities should be set out with full explanations.

Should the proposal be made by some organization, or can it be made by a private individual?
Mr. LaFLECHE: From a school or from some well-known person, a resident.

Or a member of parliament?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Yes, of course.

I have a matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. In 1941 there was in his department an item which amounted to the sum of $50,000. It was a revolving fund in connection with an organization known as the civilian technical corps. All the expenditures made from the fund were supposed to be guaranteed by the United Kingdom. There was spent from this fund in the year 1941A2 the sum of $27,000. It was
not recovered when the auditor general made his report in 1943. A further sum of $7,833 was spent in 1943. Would the minister give a short statement showing the position of this revolving fund at the present time, and what reason could be advanced for the United Kingdom not meeting the amount which had been debited to them?
Mr. LaFLECHE: The civilian technical corps came into being at the request of the British government before the United States entered the war. It was felt that a great many qualified technical Americans would be very happy to go to the British isles and serve there in undertakings requiring technical knowledge and experience. The organization was not a Canadian one. It was a United Kingdom establishment. It was placed under my department nominally. It was in Montreal under the direct supervision of the United Kingdom air mission, I believe.
The Canadian government advanced the moneys and periodically the Canadian government was reimbursed for expenditures made. I do not recall the exact standing of the account as of March 31, 1943; but I know the entire account has been paid. Thehon. member has asked, why the delay? Well, it was in putting in the bills and latterly getting them sent over to Great Britain, I understand, for final approval, or something like that. It was a revolving fund. The Canadian government has been reimbursed in full. When the United States came into the war that organization had, of course, to go out.

Then I take it that this account has been closed out and has nothing to-day with the sundry services.
Mr. LaFLECHE: No. As I recall it, there was a balance some time last year and I asked why. It was inquired into and not long ago I was told that the account had been settled.

What do you do with a balance like that?
Mr. LaFLECHE: It goes back into the consolidated revenue fund.

I think the hon. member for Vancouver South will find this of some interest. The hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough, on Monday last, the 24th of April, inquired as to
the number of certificates issued by Canadian Legion educational services. I might explain that three types of certificates are issued:
1.	Certificate for correspondence course completion.
2.	Certificate for partial completion of correspondence courses.
3.	Certificate of achievement.
1.	In this connection I should like to indicate to the committee the procedure which has been set down in order that students may qualify for these certificates. The student studies his booklets and forwards exercises to his correspondence instructor as he completes them. While his first exercise is being marked by the instructor, the student continues with paper No. 2 in order that no time may be wasted. The exercise is marked and is returned to the student, together with necessary explanations and additional instructions as to how he should procure the maximum advantage from the correspondence system of study. When the student has completed the ten papers, that is half a course, an examination is forwarded to the commanding officer who ensures that the man writes it under supervision. It is then returned to the correspondence instructor by the education officer. A similar procedure is following with the remaining ten papers and a final test is sent to him through the commanding officer on the completion of the twentieth paper. This again is written under supervision and is returned to the correspondence instructor. In all these exercises and examinations the standards of provincial departments of education are maintained. The marks gained on each of the twenty papers, plus those gained on the two supervised examinations, are averaged and the student is awarded the certificate which carries academic credit for the subject studied in all departments of education in Canada and Newfoundland.
In addition to this, the standing granted is indicated on sections 4 and 5 of his application form. Section 4 is forwarded to the officer in charge of records at national defence headquarters in Ottawa in order that it may be affixed to his permanent service records here, and section 5 is forwarded to the officer in charge of his unit in order that it may be attached to his unit papers. In this way commanding officers are made aware of the names of service personnel who are interested in advancing their own welfare. Other things being equal, we have no doubt that these are the personnel who will be chosen for whatever promotions will be available.

Certificates of partial completion are issued to students who are not primarily interested in academic credit at the present time but who, at a later date, may wish to continue their correspondence studies when the exigencies of the services so permit. In such cases a certificate of partial completion, showing the marks gained on the work actually done, is awarded in order that the student may continue his course with no difficulty at all on the production of the certificate of partial completion.
3.	Certificates of achievement are also issued for work done in Canadian Legion educational services classes. These certificates may be evaluated for academic credit in the cases where the duration of the instruction and subjects covered are acceptable to provincial departments of education, but generally they are issued for non-credit purposes. For
example, men who have studied the very elementary English course and have achieved a certain literacy in English are very proud to have their achievement recorded on certificates of this type.
Again, many service personnel make use of these classes as refresher courses and as courses to provide them with sufficient background to accept promotion within the services.
